Hey folks, on behalf of the TFT and Riftbound teams, I wanted to share a few thoughts on today’s Convergence Fest Attendee Pass General Sale.

With both TFT & Riftbound Communities showing up, we knew demand was going to be much higher than the number of passes we could offer, and we’ve been working on ways to make that experience better for players.

For our Riftbound players, this probably isn’t your first experience with us working through ticketing challenges this year. Over the last year, we’ve moved ticketing platforms multiple times, scaled up our Regional Qualifiers to nearly double the capacity of where we started in Houston, and launched the Showdown Series to create more opportunities for players to compete.

For Convergence Fest, Fan First was a new tool, and a big step for us. It was our first time using player activity, such as in-store & online play, to ensure active players got an opportunity to get tickets without having to race through checkout. That worked, allowing us to get thousands of tickets into players’ hands before the General Sale.

But we missed at the last mile today. The execution of the General Sale, an already-limited ticket offer, did not meet the experience we wanted to provide, and to make it worse, the things we said in the moment didn’t match the experience we delivered. We know there are a lot of players who really wanted to be there.

So here’s what we have planned next:

⏭️ We’ll have one final sale in November with any refunded tickets and any additional capacity we’re able to create. We expect this to be a small sale, and we’ll share more details on timing and availability once we have them.

⏭️ We’ve also started a larger effort to explore how we can take more ownership of ticketing and become less reliant on third-party platforms. It’s early, but we know there’s more we can do beyond Fan First to connect players with tickets and make these experiences better.

We know General Sale today was frustrating, and we’re sorry we didn’t deliver the experience you deserved.

For everyone who will be in Vegas, I’ll see you there. And if you’re around the Riftbound Regional Qualifier in LA this weekend, I’ll be there this afternoon and all day tomorrow. Please feel free to pull me aside, ask questions, or share your feedback. I’m always happy to chat and listen.

Thank you for all your interest, feedback, and care. We really appreciate you sticking with us and continuing to support our TFT and Riftbound communities.

The Emerging Epidemic of Early-Onset Parkinson’s Disease: Environmental Etiology, Gut-Brain Axis Dysbiosis, and Targeted Phytochemical Interventions

Monday, September 28, 2026
Dr. Joel Rutkowski

Abstract

Parkinson’s disease (PD) has transitioned from a sporadic condition of late adulthood to the fastest-growing neurological disorder globally, marked by a sharp upward trend in Early-Onset Parkinson’s Disease (EOPD) among individuals under 50. Longitudinal data spanning from 1940 to 2026 demonstrates that while monogenic inherited mutations account for under 10 percentof total cases, chronic exposure to synthetic agricultural toxicants, chlorinated solvents, and atmospheric particulates drives the majority of neurodegenerative cascades. This comprehensive review synthesizes historical environmental trends, details the gut-brain axis mechanisms driving EOPD, and evaluates the therapeutic potential of microgreens alongside botanical therapeutics—specifically Yaupon tea, Stinging Nettle, and Moringa leaf—as accessible, neuroprotective dietary strategies.

Environmental Etiology v. Nutritional Deficit (1940–2026)

Post-World War II agricultural and industrial expansion marked an inflection point in population-wide neurotoxin exposure. The decades between 1940 and 1970 saw the widespread deployment of synthetic organochlorine pesticides and chlorinated industrial degreasing solvents like trichloroethylene (TCE). Between 1980 and 2010, cellular toxicological models isolated specific pathways—such as mitochondrial Complex I inhibition—demonstrating how environmental chemicals directly disrupt cellular energy production in central dopaminergic networks.

Epidemiological tracking through 2026 indicates that the global incidence of EOPD has more than doubled. This acceleration is driven primarily by environmental bioaccumulation rather than genetic drift. Persistent agricultural agents (including Paraquat and Rotenone), combined with airborne fine particulate matter (PM2.5), breach or bypass the blood-brain barrier. These toxicants trigger chronic microglial activation and severe oxidative stress within the substantia nigra pars compacta. Concurrently, modern dietary shifts toward highly processed foods lacking cellular antioxidants leave the central nervous system vulnerable to persistent environmental exposure.

The Gut-Brain Axis and Preventive Nutrition

The gut-brain pathway plays a fundamental role in early disease manifestation. Ingested agricultural residues and industrial contaminants disrupt the gut microbiome, provoking intestinal hyperpermeability. Toxicants induce pathological misfolding of alpha-synuclein proteins directly within the enteric nervous system. These misfolded proteins propagate to the brain via retrograde transport along the vagus nerve long before motor deficits appear.

Preventative nutrition must focus on fortifying endogenous cellular defenses:

Nrf2 Pathway Activation:Upregulating the Nuclear Factor Erythroid 2-Related Factor 2 (Nrf2) transcription pathway stimulates endogenous production of superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and glutathione peroxidase.

Mitochondrial Support:Polyphenols and lipid-soluble antioxidants prevent electron leakage across the inner mitochondrial membrane, neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

Gut Barrier Preservation:Prebiotic fibers and phytochemicals foster short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, strengthening tight junction proteins in the intestinal lining to suppress systemic neuroinflammation.

Microgreens as a Targeted Phytochemical Strategy

Microgreens—cotyledon-stage seedlings harvested within 7 to 21 days of germination—offer a concentrated dietary countermeasure. These young plants yield significantly higher concentrations of bioavailable secondary metabolites than mature plants.

Sulforaphane and Glucosinolates:Cruciferous microgreens (such as broccoli and radish) contain up to 10 to 100 times the glucoraphanin concentration found in mature counterparts. Cellular disruption converts glucoraphanin into sulforaphane, a potent natural activator of the Nrf2-ARE pathway that shields dopaminergic neurons from pesticide-induced toxicity.

Polyphenolic Iron Chelation:Polyphenols present in red cabbage and amaranth microgreens scavenge free radicals and chelate univalent metal ions, slowing iron-induced lipid peroxidation in central brain tissues.

Concentrated Carotenoids:Lutein and beta-carotene embedded in young plant tissues protect mitochondrial lipid membranes from oxidative degradation without requiring heavy fiber breakdown during digestion.

Complementary Botanical Therapeutics: Yaupon Tea, Stinging Nettle, and Moringa Leaf

Integrating specific functional botanicals alongside microgreens provides additional neuroprotective pathways against environmental neurotoxicants:

Yaupon Tea (Ilex vomitoria):Native to North America, Yaupon leaf yields high concentrations of chlorogenic acids, rutin, theobromine, and moderate caffeine. Its rich polyphenol profile acts as a systemic radical scavenger, suppressing glial activation and neuroinflammatory cascades. Theobromine supports synaptic plasticity and striatal neurotransmission, while chlorogenic acids help protect dopaminergic cell populations from oxidative decay without inducing excitotoxic cell stress.

Stinging Nettle (Urtica dioica):Rich in caffeic acid derivatives, flavonoids (quercetin, kaempferol), and essential minerals, Urtica dioica helps restore autophagic flux within midbrain tissue. This activity aids in clearing pathogenic alpha-synuclein aggregates. Preclinical models confirm that Stinging Nettle inhibits caspase-3 apoptotic cascades, normalizes depleted striatal neurotransmitters, and upregulates tyrosine hydroxylase—the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis.

Moringa Leaf (Moringa oleifera):Containing moringin (an isothiocyanate functional analog to sulforaphane), quercetin, and high concentrations of vitamins C and E, Moringa leaf exhibits profound anti-inflammatory and neurotransmitter-modulating effects. Moringin potently activates the Nrf2-ARE antioxidant pathway, defending neuronal mitochondria against Complex I toxins. Furthermore, Moringa oleifera extracts suppress NF-kappaB neuroinflammatory signaling, attenuate striatal dopamine depletion, and enhance synaptic plasticity under chronic toxic load.

The escalating incidence of Early-Onset Parkinson’s Disease (EOPD) marks a profound epidemiological shift, transforming a condition historically associated with late adulthood into an urgent public health crisis for younger populations. As tracked from the post-war industrial expansion through 2026, the data confirms that EOPD is not primarily a disease of genetic inevitability—monogenic mutations account for a small minority of cases—but rather the cumulative consequence of environmental bioaccumulation, chronic exposure to synthetic neurotoxins (such as Paraquat, Rotenone, and trichloroethylene), and particulate air pollution. Understanding EOPD requires looking beyond traditional paradigms to address the modern toxic load acting upon susceptible biological systems.

Discussion: The Gut-Brain Axis and the Failure of Environmental Protection

At the center of this epidemic is the gut-brain axis, serving as both the primary entry portal for environmental toxicants and the initial site of pathological neurodegeneration. Ingested agricultural residues and industrial solvents compromise intestinal barrier integrity, instigating localized inflammation that triggers the pathological misfolding of alpha-synuclein within the enteric nervous system. Through retrograde axonal transport via the vagus nerve, these toxic aggregates advance to the central nervous system long before classical motor symptoms manifest.

This mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability in modern human physiology: humanity's evolutionary adaptations are being outpaced by the sheer volume of synthetic compounds introduced into the food, water, and air supplies over the past eight decades. Furthermore, modern dietary trends characterized by processed foods devoid of cellular antioxidants strip the central nervous system of its intrinsic buffering capacity. Consequently, contemporary medical strategies can no longer rely solely on late-stage symptomatic management (such as dopamine replacement). Effective intervention demands upstream prophylaxis—neutralizing oxidative stress and preventing neurotoxic cascades before irreversible neuronal cell death occurs within the substantia nigra pars compacta.

Final Thoughts: Integrating Dietary Biotherapeutics for Neuroprotection

To combat this environmental neurodegenerative crisis, a paradigm shift toward targeted, food-as-medicine interventions is essential. Concentrated nutritional strategies—specifically utilizing high-potency microgreens alongside specialized botanical therapeutics like Yaupon tea, Stinging Nettle, and Moringa leaf—offer a pragmatic, accessible countermeasure. By supplying high concentrations of bioactive compounds like sulforaphane, moringin, and chlorogenic acids, these functional foods directly upregulate the Nrf2-ARE antioxidant pathway, support mitochondrial energy production, suppress microglial activation, and aid in cellular autophagic clearance.

Ultimately, reversing the trajectory of EOPD requires a dual approach: rigorous regulatory reform to curb population-wide exposure to persistent synthetic neurotoxins, and proactive nutritional defense to shield the human nervous system. By strengthening the gut barrier and fortifying endogenous cellular resistance through targeted phytochemistry, medicine can offer renewed hope against the environmental pressures shaping the future of neurological health.

"The idea that a Commonwealth is made up of a number of small kingdoms, out of which a man and a woman become the king and Queen and in which they exercise A reasonable authority, subject to the common sense of the Commonwealth, until those under their care grow up to found similar kingdoms and exercise similar authority. This is the social structure of mankind, far older than all its records and more universal than all of its religions;  And all attempts to alter it are mere talk and Tomfoolery.

There is undoubtedly something to be said against domesticity and in favor of the general drift towards life in hotels, clubs, colleges, communal settlements, and the rest;  Order for a social life organized on the plan of the great commercial system of our time. But the truly extraordinary suggestion Is often made that this escape from the home  is an escape into greater freedom. The change is actually offered as favourable to liberty.... But the main point is that the world outside the home is now under a rigid discipline and routine and it is only inside the home that there Is really a place for individuality and liberty.  Anyone stepping out of the front door is obliged to step into a procession, all going the same way and to a great extent even obliged to wear the same uniform. 

So that even if we consider the parents alone as independent princes, and the children merely as subjects, the relative freedom of the family can and often does work to the advantage of those subjects. But it's so long as the children are children, they will always be the subjects of somebody. The question is whether they are to be distributed naturally under their natural princess, as the old phrase went, who normally feel for them what nobody else will feel, a natural affection. It seems to me clear that this normal distribution gives the largest amount of liberty to the largest number of people. 

My complaint of the anti domestic drift is that it is Unintelligent. People do not know what they are doing; Because they do not know what they are undoing."

-G.K. Chesterton

LET US EXTEND A HELPING HAND TO OUR TEMPLE PRIESTS 
Just pause for a minute… and open your heart.
We go to a temple.
We have Darshan of Swami.
We perform Archana.
We offer Abhishekam.
We put our offerings into the Hundi.
We pray for our family… our health… our children's future… our prosperity.
But…
Do we ever stop and think about the person who stands behind that Sanctum every single day?
The Kurukkal…
The person who wakes up before sunrise…
Who opens the temple doors…
Who cleans the Sanctum…
Who lights the lamp…
Who rings the bell…
Who chants the Mantras…
Who performs Abhishekam…
Who prepares and offers Naivedyam…
And who, with folded hands, prays for our families before Swami.
And then…
He goes back home.
Perhaps to a house with a leaking roof.
Perhaps to an empty kitchen.
Perhaps to medicines that need to be purchased.
Perhaps to a child's school fees waiting to be paid.
Perhaps to an ageing wife who needs treatment.
Perhaps to his own tired and ageing body.
Yet the next morning, he is back again.
Because there is one thought in his heart:
“Swami's Puja must never stop.”
Especially in the small, interior villages of Tamil Nadu, there are temples where only a handful of devotees visit.
There may be little income.
There may be no regular support.
There may be almost no facilities.
But…
THE PUJA CONTINUES.
The lamp continues to burn.
The bell continues to ring.
The Mantras continue to echo.
Because one Kurukkal refuses to abandon his Kainkaryam.
Sometimes, he may not even know where his next month's income will come from.
But he knows one thing:
Swami must be worshipped.
That is his dedication.
That is his Dharma.
That is his Kainkaryam.
And perhaps…
we can become the support that he desperately needs.
We can provide groceries for a month.
We can provide oil for the temple lamp and Abhishekam.
We can provide Puja materials.
We can help with medical expenses.
We can support a child's education.
We can repair a small portion of a damaged priest's house.
 We can help with an urgent family need.
It may be only a few hundred rupees for us.
But for them…
it may mean food for a family.
It may mean medicine for an elderly priest.
It may mean a child's school fee being paid.
It may mean a lamp continuing to burn.
And above all…
It may tell a Kurukkal:
“You are not alone. We are with you.”
We go to the temple to receive blessings from Swami.
They remain in the temple to serve Swami.
Let us therefore serve those who serve Him.
 The lamp they light should never go out because of poverty.
The daily Puja should never stop because the Kurukkal has no means to survive.
A family that has dedicated its life to Swami should never feel forgotten.
Remember…
Protecting a temple is not merely about protecting its walls, Gopuram or Vimanam.
A temple can have a magnificent Gopuram.
It can have a newly renovated Sanctum.
It can have beautiful stonework.
But…
Who will perform the Nitya Puja if there is no Kurukkal?
Who will light the lamp?
Who will chant the Mantras?
Who will offer Naivedyam?
Who will stand before Swami and pray for us?
That is why…
KURUKKAL FIRST… THEN THE TEMPLE.
Let us wipe away a Kurukkal's tears.
Let us reduce a family's burden.
Let us support a child's education.
Let us help an elderly priest obtain medical treatment.
Let us put groceries into an empty kitchen.
Let us put oil into a temple lamp.
Let us ensure that the Nitya Puja continues without interruption.
This is not charity alone.
This is Kainkaryam.
This is Dharma.
This is our responsibility towards our Sanatana heritage.
We seek Swami's blessings every day.
Let us also remember the person who stands before Swami every day seeking nothing for himself, but praying for all of us.
A small contribution from us can become a great support in his life.
Let us not wait for them to ask.
Let us reach them before they are forced to give up.
Save Our Priests.
Support Our Kurukkals.
Keep the Nitya Puja Alive.
Let the Temple Lamp Continue to Burn.

1.  Body of Christ ≠ “no visible Church.” A body has members and order. Christ built a Church (Mt 16:18), told us to take disputes “to the Church” (Mt 18:17), and that Church bound the flock at Jerusalem (Acts 15). 

“Man-made” fits Luther, Calvin, and every denomination that starts with a man’s name. It doesn’t fit the Church that already existed when the New Testament was written - and that later defined which books are the New Testament.

2.  “People, not a building” is a straw man. No Catholic says the Church is the brick. The building is where the people gather.

3.  Living stones (1 Pet 2:5) is Catholic doctrine. A spiritual house does not cancel a visible people with bishops, altars, and public worship. Israel was a priestly people and had a temple.

4.  Christ owns the Church (Acts 20:28). The Pope doesn’t. He’s a steward. Joseph ran Egypt; Pharaoh still owned it. Jn 21:15–17 is Christ telling a man to feed His sheep.

5.  Christ is the one Head. A body can have one Head in heaven and a visible center on earth. Keys (Mt 16:18–19), “strengthen your brethren” (Lk 22:32), “feed my sheep” (Jn 21:17). “Headed by a mere man” is not the claim.

6.  One Redeemer - mediator: Christ (1 Tim 2:5). The same chapter tells you to intercede (1 Tim 2:1). James tells the sick to call the elders (Jas 5:14–16). If “no earthly mediators” were absolute, you wouldn’t need a pastor or a baptizer.

7.  “You are all brothers” (Mt 23:8) condemns pride, not offices. Paul calls himself father (1 Cor 4:15). The NT installs overseers (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5) and says obey your leaders (Heb 13:17). Brotherhood and hierarchy started on day one.

8.  Royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:9) is the baptismal priesthood. We teach it. Israel was already a kingdom of priests (Ex 19:6) and still had Levites. “Do this in memory of me” plus laying on of hands is the ministerial priesthood. All believers are priestly. Not all offer the Eucharist.

You took a Catholic sentence, added “therefore no bishops / no Pope / no sacraments / no visible Church,” and pretend the “therefore” is in the verse. It isn’t. 

The verses describe the Church we already claim. 

They don’t describe a loose association that began 1,500 years late and then calls the original “forbidden.”

A Phoenix repairman is helping keep vintage pinball machines in play as collectors rediscover the tactile appeal of the game.

Dean Kenyon, 62, grew up dropping in a quarter, hitting start, and sending the steel ball flying.

As a former Intel equipment technician with a degree in electronics, he later trained under one of the best pinball mechanics in the Phoenix area. In 2001, he launched Arizona Pinball Repair.

Today, Kenyon repairs and rebuilds machines for businesses and private collectors, running one of the few specialized pinball repair operations left in Arizona.

Pinball was huge in the 1980s and 1990s, but video and online gaming largely replaced many of the old machines. Fewer than a dozen specialized repair shops remain in Arizona. Yet at a Maryland retailer, inquiries grew from 15 in 2021 to 199 in 2024, and physical machines overtook virtual versions in 2026.

For many players, part of pinball’s greatest appeal is that it offers something screens cannot.

Evan Phillippe of the Pacific Pinball Museum said older machines remain cheaper than new ones, parts are still available, and they can be highly reliable once repaired. He also said playing well requires enough focus to provide a break from smart devices and constant screen exposure. The museum’s weekly pinball league grew four times larger after COVID.

Pinball has been part of American popular culture for generations.

It evolved from an 18th-century tabletop game into coin-operated machines by the 1930s, survived decades of bans in many U.S. cities, and surged again in the 1990s. “The Addams Family” machine, released in 1991, remains the best-selling pinball machine of all time, and Kenyon still keeps one in his dining room.

Some customers collect dozens of machines, while others seek out the exact games they remember from their younger years.

For Kenyon, the thrill of chasing a high score never gets old.

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. text:
Mercy.

In his autobiography, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee details the tragedy of his first wife’s horrific accident. Carol Ann was riding on their property in Fernvale, Tennessee one afternoon in the summer of 2000 with their four-year-old daughter, Sarah Kate.

Lee had just arrived home from work in time to see his wife and daughter riding off together on their horse. A perfect, idyllic afternoon. Or so it would seem.

Sometime later, Lee spotted his young daughter wandering by herself. Curious, he went to her and learned there had been an accident. Rushing to find his wife, he found gut-wrenching tragedy instead. Carol Ann was unconscious and seriously wounded. Both she and Sarah Kate had been thrown from the horse. Miraculously, Sarah Kate was fine, but Carol Ann had struck her head.

Though rushed to the hospital, Carol Ann succumbed to her head injuries four days later, leaving Bill Lee in a state of shock. Carol Ann was only 40 years old. They had four children — Jessica, Jacob, Caleb, and Sarah Kate.

Lee ran the family business — The Lee Company. That was his job, his duty, his contribution to his family. Carol Ann managed the home, cared for the kids. How could he possibly do any of this without her?

A man of faith, Lee reflected on the Book of Job, specifically chapters 38 and 39 — chapters he had been reading and reflecting on with Carol Ann just a few weeks earlier, on their family vacation to Yellowstone. Job, a good and faithful servant of God, is beset by numerous tragedies to test his faith. When Job asks God, “Why me?” God responds: “Brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me… Do you know when the mountain goats give birth?” (Job 38:3; 39:1)

Now it was Lee plaintively asking, Why me, God? Where was the love of God in a time such as this? Where was mercy? The Book of Job would play a significant role in Bill Lee’s life going forward.

Lee took an extended leave from his company to take on the duties of full-time fatherhood. His eldest, Jessica, was fourteen and could certainly help out some, but she was wounded herself. Losing one’s mother at any age is horrible, but for an adolescent girl, it was too much to bear. The twins, only nine years old, were just as devastated. And for Sarah Kate…

The broken family trudged on with much help from extended family, friends, their church, and their faith in God, but the nights were long and lonely for Lee. As he recounts: “Because I neglected my company for the sake of my children my business got into terrible shape — I had to sell half of it — and then my oldest daughter tried to take her life because she missed her mother so badly. (There were many nights when the motherless family would cry together and sleep together on the floor in the family room.) So, yeah, I know some of what Job went through but, like Job, my faith just got deeper and deeper. Without Jesus Christ I would have been crushed for the rest of my life.”

Within a year, tragedy would strike his household again when Jessica, now fifteen, could no longer bear the loss and attempted to take her own life. Mercifully, she survived. It would be several more years before things improved.

But they did improve. Like Job, Bill Lee saw a restoration of his family, his business, his standing. It is not an exaggeration to say Bill Lee experienced almost all that Job suffered — and then experienced his restoration.

His business exploded. Over 1,200 employees, revenues into the hundreds of millions. His eldest daughter grew up, married, and gave him three grandchildren — grandchildren that, but for God’s mercy, wouldn’t be here today. And mercifully, God gave Bill Lee a wife. Maria was his son Caleb’s teacher, and a track coach to Jessica. She was already known to the family, trusted, eventually loved as part of it. Bill and Maria married in 2008.

Bill’s family had been restored — just as it had been for Job. But the loss of what once had been remains. A hole. A person, a life-partner — a wife gone forever. Carol Ann was no longer in Bill Lee’s life.

When Job asks God, “Why me?” his friends offer their own answers. Job displeased God. Job was disobedient. Job was receiving his just reward. Job’s wife was more direct: “Just curse God and die.”

Bill Lee’s tragedy did not end on the afternoon Carol Ann was thrown from the horse. That was only the start of it. What followed was years, not days — his business, neglected while he tried to be both parents at once, fell into “terrible shape,” bad enough that he had to sell half of it. A year after losing her mother, his oldest daughter, fifteen, tried to take her own life, and survived. He describes nights the whole motherless family spent crying together on the floor, because none of them could bear to be alone with it. By his own account, it was years before things meaningfully improved. That is not a single bad afternoon he then got over. That is a sustained, compounding ordeal that tested him for the better part of a decade — grief, financial collapse, and the terror of nearly losing a second family member, one on top of the other.

There is another story worth setting beside his. Her name is Christa Gail Pike. She is currently the only woman on death row in Tennessee, sentenced to die for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a crime she committed at eighteen years old. She is now scheduled to be executed on September 30, 2026 — unless Bill Lee, in his capacity as governor, chooses to grant her clemency. Whatever judgment is owed for what she did, there is also a life that preceded it, and it is worth knowing before asking what mercy might mean here.

Job had a life. He was favored by God. He was tested in ways we would regard as horrific. Bill Lee had a life. From all outward appearances, he was favored by God — a successful family business, college, a wife, four healthy children. Then Bill Lee was tested in ways we would regard as horrific.

Christa Pike’s story is unlike Job’s, and unlike Bill Lee’s. She had a life, but one would look at it and conclude she was not favored by God. Born to an alcoholic mother and an abusive father, Christa knew none of the favored aspects of life enjoyed by Job — or Bill Lee. Her lot was horror from the very beginning. She was born with fetal alcohol syndrome, a condition she did not choose and could not have prevented, shaped before birth by harm that came from the person meant to protect her. It did not stop there. The neglect and abuse continued through her childhood — the ordinary architecture of a life that should have corrected course instead reinforcing, year after year, the idea that she was worth nothing and owed nothing. Nobody arrives at eighteen a killer by accident. Something builds that. In Christa Pike’s case, what built it was in place before she could talk, and it never let up.

This does not excuse what she did to Colleen Slemmer. Nothing excuses that, and nothing here is offered as an excuse. But it answers a different question than guilt — it answers where she came from, what she was given to work with, and it is the question mercy has always depended on being asked.

text:
🚨WOW!!!

An 81-year-old man was hauling heavy suitcases up a flight of stairs, 14 HOURS A DAY, to pay for his wife's CANCER TREATMENT...

...then the woman at the top of those stairs opened her door, heard his story, and raised him $600,000 to GO HOME to be with his wife!!!! ❤️

His name is Don Johnson.

He's 81 years old, from The Colony, Texas, just outside Dallas.

His wife Josephine has been by his side for 57 YEARS. She's fighting an aggressive cancer.

Three years ago, when the medical bills started piling up, Don went looking for work.

He tried Amazon. He tried Walmart. Nobody would take him.

So he became an independent contractor delivering lost airline luggage to people's front doors.

Sometimes 14 hours a day. Hundreds of miles in a single shift. Driving as far as OKLAHOMA to get a bag to its owner.

He put over 200,000 MILES on his own car doing it.

At 81 years old.

"I appreciate what we do get from insurance, but it doesn't cover it all. And cancer treatment is very expensive."

Then on a September day he dropped a suitcase on the steps outside a home in The Colony.

A woman named Erin Howell heard the noise on her door cam and came outside.

She offered to help carry it, and she asked him a simple question: why is a man your age doing this?

His answer: "It's the only job that will hire me."

Then he told her about Josephine.

Erin could have wished him well and gone back inside.

Instead she started a GoFundMe and a TikTok page called "Help Don Retire."

She wrote that at an age when he should be resting by his wife's side, he was out on the highway lifting bags to keep her alive.

The goal was $150,000.

It blew past that in DAYS.

Then $281,000.
Then $370,000.
Now more than $600,000 and still climbing.

More than ELEVEN THOUSAND people gave.

But here's the part that got me...

Right before all of this, Don's car had started breaking down and he'd already been forced to cut back his hours.

He was running out of road.

And that's exactly when a stranger he'd talked to for five minutes knocked on the whole country's door and AMERICA showed up.

"I left and thought I'd never see her again," Don said. "And it was an amazing thing she did for me, for us."

His wife, Josephine says after 57 years, she's watching "for better or worse" happen right in front of her.

"I'm so happy that he turned out to be the man he is."

And Don? He's not talking about himself.

"I love her dearly, and I just want her to be well. It restores my faith in people. For her and others to do for me, that was a miracle. I look forward to the day that I can help people just like I'm being helped now."

He never asked for a dime.
He just kept carrying the bags.

GOD BLESS Don and Josephine Johnson, and GOD BLESS Erin Howell.

THIS IS THE AMERICA I KNOW!!! 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

WASHINGTON SAYS IT WANTS A STRONGER YEN. TOKYO GETS ITS FIRST FULL LOOK SUNDAY NIGHT:

Every stock market in Asia is closed until Sunday evening, US time, and the prices they left behind are not equally fresh. Tokyo finished Friday with the Nikkei 225 at 66,364.20, +850.21 / +1.30%, its fifth straight gain. Hours after that close, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he and Japan's finance minister had discussed "the desirability of a strong yen," and the yen stretched its best day since September 7.

The verdict: Tokyo has the most catching up to do of any Asian market when it reopens at 8pm ET Sunday. Nothing went wrong in Japan. But a stronger yen shrinks what Japan's exporters earn abroad once those sales are counted back home, and exporters have done much of the lifting in Tokyo's rally.

How Friday unfolded:
- Tokyo's morning: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said President Trump raised concerns about the weak yen when he met Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in New York this week. Tokyo rose 1.3% anyway.
- Late Friday Tokyo time, after its market had closed: Katayama and Bessent held a call, and Japan's Finance Ministry said they agreed "yen undervaluation is a matter of concern."
- The yen, counted in yen per dollar - fewer means a stronger yen: about 158.8 at Tokyo's open, 158.1 at its close, 157.2 by the end of New York trading.

More than half of that roughly 1% gain came after Tokyo shut, on a day the dollar also slipped against most major currencies. Tokyo traded the first warning. It has not traded the second one, or the stronger yen that followed.

Why a few words carry weight now: this summer the US and Japan bought yen together for the first time since 1998, and Japan spent 15.4 trillion yen, about $97.4B, in the month through August 26. Traders watch 160 yen per dollar as the line where the odds of another round climb. The yen had weakened four days straight this week, to about 158.9 on Thursday.

Friday's Tokyo gain came from chipmakers and banks, helped by cheaper oil and a pause in the worldwide bond selloff. Banks like higher interest rates, and Japan's 10-year government bond yield sits near its highest since 1996, at 3.077%, -0.005 point on Friday. The chip-equipment makers sell much of what they build overseas. They are the part of the rally most exposed to a stronger yen. Tokyo's benchmark is still about 8% under its June 22 record of 72,353.96.

The same yen cuts the other way for Americans who own Japan through a fund. iShares MSCI Japan ETF (EWJ) at $97.93, +$2.12 / +2.21% on Friday, gained more than Tokyo did, because each Japanese share was worth more in dollars. A stronger yen pays the dollar-based owner and squeezes the exporters inside the fund.

Hong Kong is the opposite case: its closing price already reflects its news. It was the only China market open Friday. Shanghai and Shenzhen were shut for the Mid-Autumn Festival, and Stock Connect, the link mainland investors use to buy Hong Kong shares, was closed with them. The Hang Seng ended at 24,510.09, -251.04 / -1.01%, its third straight loss, as Chinese President Xi Jinping's Washington visit wrapped up with the trade truce extended two months, to January 10, and no deal on tariffs, rare earths or chip export limits. Technology shares led the slide: Hong Kong's tech index at 4,311.78, -49.35 / -1.13%. US traders did not argue: iShares China Large-Cap ETF (FXI) at $33.96, -$0.28 / -0.82% on Friday. The Shanghai Composite last traded Thursday, at 3,888.37, -48.15 / -1.22%. Mainland markets reopen Monday for just three sessions, then close October 1-7 for the National Day holiday.

US stock futures stopped at 5pm ET Friday and reopen at 6pm ET Sunday, two hours before Tokyo. Their final moves, each since Thursday's close: S&P 500 futures at 7,805.75, +38.75 / +0.50%; Nasdaq-100 futures at 30,921.75, +155 / +0.50%; Dow futures at 52,180.00, +463 / +0.90%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,859.90, +3.10 / +0.11%. Those are Friday's gains, not a forecast for Monday.

Why a yen move matters on Wall Street at all: speed. In the summer of 2024 the yen rose more than 10% in about a month, and investors who had borrowed cheaply in yen to buy assets elsewhere sold in a rush. On August 5, 2024, Tokyo's benchmark fell 12.4%, its worst day since 1987, and US stocks fell about 3%. Friday's 1% is nowhere near that pace. What is new is that the push for a stronger yen now carries the US Treasury's name.

Sunday night, Eastern time:
- 6:00pm: US stock futures, oil and gold reopen - the first prices after any US answer to Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the US lifts its naval blockade and waives sanctions on Iranian oil. West Texas Intermediate crude, the US oil benchmark, finished Friday at $92.44 a barrel, -$2.17 / -2.29% from Thursday's settlement. Japan imports nearly all its oil, so cheaper crude helps Tokyo too.
- 8:00pm: Tokyo and Seoul open. Seoul returns from the Chuseok harvest holiday; the KOSPI last traded Wednesday, at 7,080.92, +63.01 / +0.90%.
- 9:00pm: Taipei, shut Friday for the Mid-Autumn Festival; the Taiex last traded Thursday, at 48,024.60, -132.69 / -0.28%.
- 9:30pm: Hong Kong and Shanghai.

The number that decides Tokyo's open is the yen, now about 157.2 per dollar. Holding there or strengthening means exporters open with a headwind. A slide back toward Thursday's 158.9 would say traders doubt Washington will back its words with yen-buying.

Tokyo built a five-day winning streak on a weak yen. Sunday night it trades, for the first time, with the US Treasury openly asking for a stronger one.
